title: 1 Enoch
subtitle: visions in the name of the man who walked with God, in five books
lead: 1 Enoch claims to be the visions of Enoch, the seventh man from Adam, who "walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). It tells how rebel angels, the Watchers, came down to earth, fathered giants and taught people sin; how Enoch toured heaven, the underworld and the ends of the earth; how the sun, moon and stars keep God's calendar; how all of history will run to a final judgment; and how a heavenly Son of Man will sit on God's throne. It has 108 chapters and 1,063 verses.

It is not in most Bibles. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches count it as Scripture, and it survives complete only in their ancient language, Ge'ez. Jews, Catholics, the other Orthodox churches and Protestants do not count it as Scripture. Yet it matters to all of them. Jude 14–15 quotes it, eleven copies in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and it shows what many Jews believed about angels, evil and the end of the world in the centuries before Jesus. Most scholars see it as five Jewish works written between about 300 BC and the time of Jesus and collected under Enoch's name.
facts: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches (and the Beta Israel, Ethiopia's Jews). Not Scripture for Jews, Catholics, Eastern Orthodox, other Oriental Orthodox or Protestants.
The book presents itself as the words of Enoch (1:1–2). Ethiopian Orthodox tradition: Enoch himself. Most scholars: several unknown Jewish scribes writing in Enoch's name.

Most scholars: Book of the Watchers (1–36), about 300–200 BC; Astronomical Book (72–82), by about 200 BC, perhaps earlier; Dream Visions (83–90), about 165–160 BC; Epistle of Enoch (91–105), about 170–100 BC; Parables (37–71), probably about 40 BC to AD 70; chapters 106–107 by the 100s BC; chapter 108 probably last of all.

Aramaic for at least the Watchers, the Astronomical Book, the Dream Visions and the Epistle (Dead Sea Scrolls). The Parables' first language is unknown, Aramaic or Hebrew. A few scholars have argued for Hebrew in other parts too.

Ge'ez (complete, in well over a hundred manuscripts, none older than the 1400s); Greek (about a third of the book, AD 300s–500s copies); Aramaic fragments from Qumran (about 200 BC to the turn of the era); small pieces in Coptic, Latin and Syriac.
Apocalypse (a revealed vision of heaven and the end), with journeys, an animal allegory, a calendar treatise, parables, woes and blessings
authorship: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, received these visions and wrote them down, as the book says (1:1–2; 82:1–2; 92:1). He handed his books to his son Methuselah, and they came through Noah to later generations. Jude confirms this when he writes that Enoch "prophesied" (Jude 14). For the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches, the book belongs to the Old Testament, is read with the prophets, and is explained in the church's traditional commentary (andəmta). Ethiopian teachers point out that the early church fathers who rejected it gave reasons of caution, not proof that Enoch did not speak.

Almost all scholars, including most Christian and Jewish scholars, see the book as a library of at least five Jewish writings composed between about 300 BC and the first century AD and later bound together. Each part has its own style and concerns. The Aramaic fragments from Qumran show that four of the parts existed by the 100s BC, while the Parables (37–71) are missing at Qumran and are later. The writers used a name from the distant past, as other Jewish writings of the period did (for example 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch), a practice called pseudonymity. Many think this was a literary convention, a way to claim the authority of ancient wisdom, not an attempt to deceive. The Book of the Watchers draws on Genesis 6:1–4, so it was written after Genesis, not before it; the Astronomical Book's interest in the solar year may reflect Enoch's 365 years (Genesis 5:23).

Some scholars (J. T. Milik, Gabriele Boccaccini and others) think the parts came from one ongoing scribal movement, sometimes called "Enochic Judaism," which kept adding to its Enoch books. Milik argued that the Parables were a Christian work of about AD 270; almost no one holds that now, since the Parables show no clear Christian marks. Some conservative Christian scholars suggest the book may keep a few very old traditions about Enoch, as Jude's quotation might imply, while still being written down late.

audience.to: Each of the five books had its own first readers, all of them Jews in the land of Israel (and perhaps in the eastern Jewish world) between about 300 BC and the first century AD. The Book of the Watchers (1–36) and the Astronomical Book (72–82) were written for learned priestly or scribal circles in Judea under Greek rule, people who cared about the calendar, the Temple's purity and the origin of evil. The Dream Visions (83–90) were written for faithful Jews during the persecution of Antiochus IV and the Maccabean revolt (about 167–160 BC), when the Temple had been defiled. The Epistle (91–105) is addressed to "my children" and "the righteous": a group of pious, often poor Jews who felt oppressed by rich and powerful people, perhaps other Jews. The Parables (37–71) were written for Jews under Roman rule and Herod's dynasty (if the usual date is right), when "the kings and the mighty" seemed to own the land. Later most of its parts were read by Jews at Qumran (the Parables are not found there), the book was read by early Christians in Greek, and from the Aksumite period on by Ethiopian Christians, who still read it.
audience.why: The writers wanted to answer the hardest questions faithful Jews faced. Why is the world so full of violence and evil? The Watchers answer: rebel angels and their giant children corrupted the earth, and God has already judged them. Why do the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer? The Epistle answers: wait, because the judgment is coming and the books are written. Has God abandoned his people under foreign kings? The Dream Visions answer: all of history, from Adam to the Maccabees, is in God's hand, and a new age is coming. Who will set things right? The Parables answer: a heavenly Chosen One, the Son of Man, already hidden with God. Enoch was the ideal person to say all this, because he lived before the Flood, walked with God and was taken to heaven alive. Knowing the readers changes the reading. The book is not a puzzle book or a collection of strange secrets. It is comfort and warning for people who felt the world was out of order, much like Daniel and Revelation.
views: Many scholars (Nickelsburg, Suter, Reed) read the Book of the Watchers as aimed in part at priests: the angels who left heaven to take wives look like priests who defiled the Temple by improper marriages (15:3–4). Others think the main target is Greek culture, with its weapons, cosmetics and magic taught by the Watchers (8:1–3).

Gabriele Boccaccini and others think one group, "Enochic Judaism," wrote and kept adding to these books, a priestly opposition to the Jerusalem establishment linked with the people of Qumran. Others (VanderKam, Collins) are more cautious: the parts share a hero and some ideas, but their readers may have been different circles over two or three centuries.

The Epistle's woes against the rich (94–100) may be aimed at wealthy Jews who sided with the Greek rulers, at Hasmonean leaders, or at Gentile oppressors. Scholars differ, and the text never names them.

For the Ethiopian Orthodox, the first audience is Enoch's own family (81:5–6; 82:1–2; 91:1) and through them every later generation; 1:2 says the vision was meant not for Enoch's own generation but for one far in the future. The book was written for the church that would one day read it.

outline: Introduction: Enoch's blessing on the chosen and the coming of God to judge (the passage Jude quotes, 1:9)
The Watchers: 200 angels under Shemihazah and Azazel come down on Mount Hermon, take wives, father giants and teach forbidden arts; God orders the Flood and their binding
Enoch carries the Watchers' petition to heaven, sees God's throne, and brings back their sentence
Enoch's journeys with the angels: the prison of the stars, the places of the dead, the tree of life, Jerusalem, paradise and the ends of the earth
The Parables (Similitudes), first parable: the coming judgment and the dwellings of the righteous
Second parable: the Head of Days and the Son of Man, the Chosen One, who judges kings
Third parable: the blessed, the judgment of the mighty, the Noah fragments, and the names of the fallen angels
Enoch is taken up; in 71:14 he is told that he is the Son of Man (meaning debated)
The Astronomical Book (Luminaries): the angel Uriel shows Enoch the laws of sun, moon and stars and a 364-day year; Enoch's charge to Methuselah
Dream Visions, first dream: the earth destroyed by flood, and Enoch's prayer
Second dream, the Animal Apocalypse: all history from Adam to the Maccabees as a story of bulls, sheep and wild beasts, ending with a white bull and a new house
The Epistle of Enoch: counsel to his children, the Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10 with 91:11–17), and woes on the sinners and comfort for the righteous
"Another book that Enoch wrote," as it calls itself: a closing word to the faithful of the last days

lenses.name: Ethiopian Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches read 1 Enoch as Scripture: a true prophecy given to Enoch, seventh from Adam, and handed down in Ge'ez with the rest of their Bible.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read it as a collection of five Jewish works written between about 300 BC and the time of Jesus under Enoch's name, and ask what each part meant to the groups that wrote and first read it.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who study how Jude, 1 and 2 Peter, Revelation, the Gospels and the early church fathers drew on Enoch's ideas: the Watchers, the Son of Man, judgment and the life to come.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: How Jews read Enoch: copied and treasured at Qumran, then set aside by the rabbis, who often read Genesis 5:24 and 6:1-4 against it, with echoes surviving in later mystical texts such as 3 Enoch.

lenses.name: Most churches: useful, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic, Orthodox (outside Ethiopia and Eritrea) and Protestant readers: an ancient witness to what Jews believed before Christ, worth reading for background, and to be tested against the Bible rather than read as the Bible.

sections.b:
Read it as a library, not as one book. Its five main parts were written at different times, in different styles, for different readers. Start with the Book of the Watchers (1–36), which explains the rest, and read Genesis 5:18–6:8 first, since the whole book grows out of those verses.

Watch for three big ideas that run through every part: evil has a history (it came through the rebel angels, 6–16), God has a plan for all time (the calendar of 72–82, the history of 85–90 and 93:1–10), and judgment is coming for the powerful who oppress the righteous (1:9; 46–48; 94–105). The notes mark where the book draws on the Hebrew Bible, where the New Testament uses it, and where it goes beyond or differs from the 66 books.

Most readers will meet the book through Jude 14–15, through Genesis 6, or through popular books about giants and fallen angels. Read it slowly and in its own setting. It is an ancient Jewish book of comfort and warning, and Christians who do not count it as Scripture can still learn from it what Jesus' first hearers already believed.

The Plain English is translated for this site from the Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic) text edited by August Dillmann in 1851, checked against the printed Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Where the older Greek or Aramaic survives, the writers read it too. Where the Ethiopic is plainly damaged and scholars agree that an older witness is right, the Plain follows the older witness and a variant note says so. R. H. Charles's English of 1917, which is free to use, was used only to check the sense.

Key terms are the same throughout: "the Watchers" (Ge'ez təguhan, Greek egrēgoroi, Aramaic 'irin), "the Lord of Spirits," "the Head of Days," "the Chosen One," and "the Son of Man," which stands for three different Ge'ez phrases that a note explains at the first of each.

1. The Book of the Watchers (1–36). The oldest part, with the Astronomical Book. It retells Genesis 6:1–4: angels called Watchers come down, marry women and father giants, who fill the earth with violence. The angels also teach metalwork, weapons, cosmetics, magic and astrology. God sends the Flood and binds the Watchers until the last judgment. Enoch is sent to tell them their doom, and then travels through the universe with angel guides. Copied at Qumran from about 200 BC on.

2. The Parables, or Similitudes (37–71). Three long "parables" (visions) about the judgment of "the kings and the mighty" by a heavenly figure called the Chosen One, the Righteous One, the Anointed One and the Son of Man, who sits on the throne of glory. It is the only part not found at Qumran or in Greek, and the most debated, because its Son of Man is so close to the Gospels.

3. The Astronomical Book, or Book of the Luminaries (72–82). The angel Uriel shows Enoch how the sun, moon and stars move through gates in the sky, and that the true year has 364 days, exactly 52 weeks. The Aramaic copies are much longer than the Ge'ez, which is a shortened form.

4. The Dream Visions (83–90). Two dreams Enoch tells Methuselah. The second, the Animal Apocalypse, retells the Bible's story from Adam to the Maccabean revolt with animals: the patriarchs are bulls, Israel is sheep, and the nations are wild animals and birds of prey. It ends with judgment, a new house for the sheep, and a white bull from whom all become white bulls again.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (91–105). Enoch's last words to his children: the Apocalypse of Weeks, which divides history into ten "weeks," and a long series of woes on the rich and the wicked with promises to the righteous, who will shine like the stars of heaven (104:2).

Appendices. Chapters 106–107 tell of Noah's wondrous birth (also found at Qumran), and chapter 108, which survives only in Ge'ez, is "another book that Enoch wrote" for the faithful of the last days.

Some scholars call the whole an "Enochic Pentateuch," five books like the five books of Moses (Milik's term); others note that the parts were joined later and unevenly.

1 Enoch is the largest and oldest of the Jewish "pseudepigrapha," writings in the name of an ancient hero. Its oldest parts are among the earliest Jewish apocalypses we have, as old as or older than Daniel. Other books built on it. Jubilees (100s BC) describes Enoch as the first to learn writing and record the signs of the sky (Jubilees 4:17–25) and retells the Watchers' story. The Genesis Apocryphon and the Book of Giants from Qumran expand it. The Damascus Document of the Qumran community names the fall of the Watchers as a warning. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs cite "the writing of Enoch" several times.

After AD 70 the rabbis did not keep it, and the Mishnah warns against reading "outside books" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). Rabbinic writers often read Genesis 5 and 6 in ways that undercut the book: Enoch was not taken to heaven but died early (Genesis Rabbah 25.1), and the "sons of God" were nobles or judges, not angels (Genesis Rabbah 26.5). Yet the Enoch traditions did not vanish. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis names Shemihazah and Azael as fallen angels, the Talmud links the scapegoat for Azazel to Uzza and Azael (Babylonian Talmud Yoma 67b), and the mystical book 3 Enoch (Sefer Hekhalot, probably 400s–600s AD or later) makes Enoch into Metatron, the great angel-scribe of heaven.

Before 1952, scholars knew 1 Enoch only from Ge'ez, Greek and a few scraps. Then Cave 4 at Qumran gave up eleven Aramaic manuscripts, published in full by J. T. Milik in 1976. Seven contain parts of the Watchers, Dream Visions and Epistle (4Q201, 4Q202, 4Q204, 4Q205, 4Q206, 4Q207, 4Q212). Four contain the Astronomical Book (4Q208, 4Q209, 4Q210, 4Q211). The oldest, 4Q208 and 4Q201, were copied around 200 BC, so their texts are older still.

The fragments show four things. First, the book is old: most of it existed before Daniel was finished. Second, it was loved: only a handful of books of the Hebrew Bible (Psalms, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus) have more copies at Qumran. Third, it was not yet one book: the Astronomical Book was copied on its own scrolls, and one scroll (4Q204) seems to hold several parts together. Fourth, the Parables are missing. No piece of 37–71 has been found, which is a main reason most scholars date them later. The Aramaic also corrects the Ge'ez in places, for example by showing that the Apocalypse of Weeks once ran in order (93:1–10, then 91:11–17).

For about a thousand years Western Christians knew 1 Enoch only by name and from Jude. In 1606 Joseph Scaliger printed the Greek excerpts of chapters 6–16 preserved by the Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus (about AD 810). Europeans heard that a whole Book of Enoch survived in Ethiopia, and a manuscript bought in the 1600s for the French scholar Peiresc turned out to be a different Ethiopian book.

In 1773 the Scottish explorer James Bruce returned from Ethiopia with three copies of the real book. He gave one to the royal library in Paris and one to the Bodleian Library in Oxford, and kept one. In 1800 Silvestre de Sacy published Latin translations of some chapters. In 1821 Richard Laurence, professor of Hebrew at Oxford and later Archbishop of Cashel, published the first English translation, The Book of Enoch the Prophet, and in 1838 the Ge'ez text. In 1851 August Dillmann published a careful Ge'ez text from five manuscripts, followed by a German translation in 1853; his text underlies this site's translation. The discovery of the Greek papyrus at Akhmim in Egypt (published 1892) added most of chapters 1–32 in Greek. R. H. Charles then produced the standard English edition and commentary (1893, revised 1912) and a critical Ge'ez text (1906), and his 1917 translation became the one most English readers know. In 1976 Milik's edition of the Qumran fragments began the modern era of study.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Jude quoted the book's thesis sentence
spec.body: Jude did not quote a stray line. 1:9 is the climax of the book's opening oracle (1:3–9), the sentence that states what the whole collection is about: God comes with his holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their harsh words. Jude needed exactly that, and his key word "ungodly" comes straight from it. If so, Jude may be pointing his readers to the whole message of a book they knew, not just borrowing a proof text, which helps explain both why the Ethiopian church took the quotation as an endorsement and why others thought it endorsed only the prophecy. Bauckham shows how closely Jude's wording tracks this passage; the suggestion that Jude chose it as the book's summary is my own.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book for people who felt like Noah
spec.body: Most parts of 1 Enoch return to Noah (the Astronomical Book is the exception): the Flood is the model of the last judgment (10:1–3; 65–67; 83–84; 106–107). The first readers lived, as they saw it, in a corrupt world just before a second great judgment. Enoch's role as the one who warns and Noah's role as the one who survives give the reader two parts to play: listen to the warning, and be the remnant God saves. Jesus uses the same pairing when he says the coming of the Son of Man will be like the days of Noah (Matthew 24:37–39). I offer this as a reading of the book's design; scholars have noted the Noah material, but not, as far as I know, framed it this way.

views: Yes. 1 Enoch (Henok) is in the Old Testament of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches, among their 81 books, and is read as the word of God given through the prophet Enoch. Bruk Ayele Asale's study shows how the church receives it as Christian Scripture, often in light of Jude 14–15.

No. The Coptic, Syrian and Armenian Orthodox churches share the Ethiopian church's faith in other ways, but 1 Enoch is not in their Bibles. In Egypt, Athanasius's Festal Letter 39 (AD 367) already asked who had made simple believers think such books belonged to Enoch, "even though no Scripture existed before Moses."

No. Augustine wrote that Enoch surely wrote some inspired things, since Jude says so, but the books under his name were rightly kept out of the canon because their origin could not be proven (City of God 15.23). The canon defined at Trent (1546) does not include it.

No. The Greek Old Testament used by the Eastern Orthodox never included it, though Greek fathers knew it and Byzantine chroniclers quoted it. Lists such as the Stichometry of Nicephorus place it among the apocrypha.

No. The Thirty-Nine Articles list the canonical books and the Apocrypha read "for example of life and instruction of manners"; 1 Enoch is in neither list, so it has no place in the church's public reading.

No. The Westminster Confession says books not inspired by God have no authority in the church and are to be used only as other human writings. Reformed writers value 1 Enoch as background, as they value Josephus.

Not part of their canon, but they hold the canon is open. Their own scripture has a long account of Enoch in the Book of Moses (Moses 6–7, in the Pearl of Great Price), which is different from 1 Enoch, and the Doctrine and Covenants (107:57) speaks of a book of Enoch to be made known in due time. Some Latter-day Saint scholars have compared the two Enoch traditions with interest.

canon.summary: 1 Enoch is Scripture for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches, which keep it in their Old Testament, and for the Beta Israel, Ethiopia's ancient Jewish community. Jews, Catholics, Eastern Orthodox, the other Oriental Orthodox churches and Protestants do not count it as Scripture, though Jude 14–15 quotes it and it was treasured at Qumran and by some early Christians.
accepted_by: Scripture. It is part of the Old Testament in the church's 81-book canon (in both the "narrow" and "broad" ways of counting it, as Cowley describes) and is read and taught with the prophets. When it was first counted as Scripture is not known. It was probably translated from Greek into Ge'ez in the Aksumite period (roughly AD 400–600), and the Ethiopian church kept copying it when the rest of the church had let it go. Well over a hundred Ge'ez manuscripts survive; the oldest are from the 1400s, and many later ones are copied together with other Old Testament books. The church also has a traditional commentary on it (andəmta).
Scripture, in the same Ge'ez Bible and 81-book canon, since this church grew out of the Ethiopian church and became self-governing in the 1990s.

Counted among their holy books. Their Bible was in Ge'ez and, as far as scholars report, included Enoch and Jubilees along with the Torah (Orit) and other books. How it was used in their worship, and how this changed after many moved to Israel, is less well documented; treat the details as uncertain.
Coptic, Syriac and Armenian Orthodox churches

Not Scripture. These Oriental Orthodox churches never placed it in their Bibles. A Coptic fragment of 93:3–8 shows it was read in Egypt, and the Syriac chronicler Michael the Syrian (1100s) quotes a passage, but as history, not as Scripture.

Not Scripture. It was never part of the Greek Old Testament. Byzantine lists (the Stichometry of Nicephorus) name it among the apocrypha, though George Syncellus quoted it as a source for early history.
Not Scripture. Never in any Latin Bible or official list. Augustine judged it outside the canon, and the Council of Trent (1546) did not include it. Catholic scholars study it widely as background.

Not Scripture, not even among the Apocrypha that some Protestants read for instruction. The Westminster Confession and the Thirty-Nine Articles leave it out entirely. Most Protestant scholars value it as background for Jude, 1 and 2 Peter and the Gospels.

Not Scripture. It is not in the Hebrew Bible, the rabbis did not copy it, and the Mishnah warns against "outside books." Some of its traditions survive in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, the Talmud and 3 Enoch.

Treasured. Eleven Aramaic copies (more than of most books of the Hebrew Bible), plus related Enoch works such as the Book of Giants and books that cite it, such as Jubilees. Whether they counted it as Scripture in the later sense is debated, since there was no closed list yet; it clearly had high authority for them.

Mixed. The Epistle of Barnabas (about 100–130) quotes Enoch, once introducing it as "Scripture" (Barnabas 16.5). Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria used its story of the Watchers. Tertullian (about 200) defended it as Scripture and blamed the Jews for rejecting it because it speaks of Christ. Origen used it but noted that the churches did not generally accept it as divine (Against Celsus 5.54). Jerome reported that many rejected Jude because it quotes Enoch (Lives of Illustrious Men 4), and Augustine set it aside (City of God 15.23). By the 400s it had dropped out of use outside Ethiopia.

Some Rastafari, some Hebrew Israelite and Hebrew Roots groups, and some independent Christians read it as inspired or as a lost book of the Bible, often through Charles's English or the "Ethiopian Bible." None of these is a church that once held it and kept it; their use is recent. Popular writers on giants and fallen angels also draw on it heavily.

provenance.b:
Scholars date each part separately, using the Qumran copies, the events it seems to describe, and its ideas.

  • Book of the Watchers (1–36): about 300–200 BC. The oldest copy, 4Q201, was made about 200–150 BC, and the text had already grown from smaller pieces (6–11 is probably older than 12–36). Most date it in the 200s BC, some in the late 300s.
  • Astronomical Book (72–82): by about 200 BC, perhaps in the 300s. The copy 4Q208 dates to about 200 BC, among the oldest Enoch manuscripts.
  • Dream Visions (83–90): about 165–160 BC. The Animal Apocalypse follows history up to a ram with a great horn who fights the birds of prey (90:9–16), widely taken as Judas Maccabeus, but not his death in 160 BC. 4Q207 and 4Q204–206 contain parts of it.
  • Epistle of Enoch (91–105): about 170–100 BC. The Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17) seems to come from just before the Maccabean revolt. 4Q212, from the 1st century BC, contains it.
  • Parables (37–71): probably about 40 BC to AD 70. They are missing from Qumran and from the Greek. They mention an invasion by Parthians and Medes (56:5–7), which many link to the Parthian invasion of 40 BC, and hot springs that punish kings (67:8–13), which some link to Herod the Great's visit to the springs at Callirrhoe. Milik's date of about AD 270 is now almost universally rejected; the Enoch Seminar of 2005 found most specialists favoring the late 1st century BC or early 1st century AD.
  • Birth of Noah (106–107): by the 100s BC (found in 4Q204). Chapter 108: found only in Ge'ez; probably the last addition, date uncertain.

The Qumran finds settled that the Watchers, the Astronomical Book, the Dream Visions, the Epistle and the Noah chapters were written in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in that era and the language of Daniel 2:4–7:28. A few scholars have argued that some parts first existed in Hebrew, and the Qumran Hebrew fragment called 1Q19 (a "Book of Noah") shows Noah material in Hebrew too, but the Aramaic copies are the earliest text we have. The language of the Parables is unknown, since no Semitic copy survives: Aramaic or Hebrew. The book then went into Greek, probably before the time of Jesus or soon after (Jude seems to know a Greek form), and from Greek into Ge'ez. Whether the Ge'ez translators also had an Aramaic copy is debated.

All from Cave 4, all fragmentary, dated by handwriting (approximate dates, mostly Milik's, which later editors have adjusted in places):

  • 4Q201 (4QEnoch-a): Watchers; about 200–150 BC.
  • 4Q202 (4QEnoch-b): Watchers; about the middle of the 100s BC.
  • 4Q204 (4QEnoch-c): Watchers, Dream Visions, Epistle and the Birth of Noah, including 1:9; late 1st century BC.
  • 4Q205 (4QEnoch-d): Watchers and Dream Visions; late 1st century BC.
  • 4Q206 (4QEnoch-e): Watchers and Dream Visions; early or middle 1st century BC.
  • 4Q207 (4QEnoch-f): Dream Visions; about 150–125 BC.
  • 4Q212 (4QEnoch-g): Epistle, including the Apocalypse of Weeks; middle or late 1st century BC.
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr-a): Astronomical Book; about 200 BC or a little earlier.
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr-b): Astronomical Book; around the turn of the era.
  • 4Q210 (4QEnastr-c): Astronomical Book; 1st century BC.
  • 4Q211 (4QEnastr-d): Astronomical Book; second half of the 1st century BC.

Other Qumran texts are related but are not copies of 1 Enoch: the Book of Giants (4Q203, 4Q530–533, 1Q23–24, 2Q26, 6Q8) and the Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20). A few tiny Greek papyrus scraps from Cave 7 (7Q4, 7Q8, 7Q12) have been identified by some scholars as Greek text of chapter 103; others disagree. A small Aramaic fragment of unknown origin (XQpapEnoch, published in 2005) contains part of chapters 8–9.

About a third of 1 Enoch survives in Greek:

  • Codex Panopolitanus (the Akhmim or Gizeh manuscript), found in a grave at Akhmim in Egypt in the 1880s and published in 1892, a parchment book of about the 500s (estimates run from the 400s to the 600s). It has 1:1–32:6, with 19:3–21:9 copied twice, bound with the Gospel of Peter and the Apocalypse of Peter.
  • George Syncellus, a Byzantine monk who wrote a world chronicle about AD 810, quoted long excerpts from chapters 6–10 and 15–16, sometimes in a form different from the Akhmim text.
  • The Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus, from the 300s, with most of 97:6–107:3 (published by Campbell Bonner in 1937), copied in one book with Melito of Sardis's Easter homily.
  • A Vatican manuscript (Vatican Greek 1809, medieval) with 89:42–49 in Greek shorthand.
  • Oxyrhynchus papyrus 2069 (300s), with a few lines that Milik identified as parts of 77–78 and 85–87, an identification some question.
  • Quotations in early Christian writers, above all 1:9 in Jude 14–15.

Only Ge'ez has the whole book. The translation was probably made from Greek in the Aksumite kingdom (about AD 400–600). The oldest surviving copies come from the 1400s, roughly a thousand years after the translation and seventeen centuries after the oldest parts were written. Scholars now know of well over a hundred manuscripts, and more keep being catalogued.

Scholars group them in two families. Ethiopic I (Charles's "alpha" group) is the older and more varied type, found in manuscripts of the 1400s–1600s such as Lake Tana 9 and several in the Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library (EMML). Ethiopic II (Charles's "beta" group) is a later revised and smoothed text, standard from about the 1600s on, which most later copies and the printed church Bible follow. Knibb's edition (1978) printed the 18th-century Rylands Ethiopic manuscript 23 with readings from others; Dillmann's text, used here, was made from a small number of later manuscripts and leans toward Ethiopic II. Where Ethiopic I, the Greek and the Aramaic agree against Ethiopic II, scholars usually follow them.

• Coptic: a fragment from Antinoe in Egypt with 93:3–8 (part of the Apocalypse of Weeks), probably from the 500s–600s, published in 1960.
  • Latin: a short excerpt of 106:1–18 in an 8th-century manuscript in the British Library (Royal 5 E XIII), identified by M. R. James in 1893, plus a Latin quotation of 1:9 in a 3rd-century treatise (Pseudo-Cyprian, Against Novatian).
  • Syriac: a short excerpt from chapter 6 in the Chronicle of Michael the Syrian (1100s).

rejected_why.b: The rabbis who shaped Judaism after AD 70 did not copy or cite 1 Enoch. The Mishnah says a person who reads the "outside books" has no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1), and later teachers explained those as books outside the 24 of the Hebrew Bible. They also answered Enoch's main claims through Genesis itself. In Genesis Rabbah 25.1 one rabbi says Enoch was a hypocrite, sometimes righteous and sometimes wicked, and was removed early before he could turn bad; others answer heretics (probably Christians) who claimed Enoch never died. In Genesis Rabbah 26.5 Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai curses anyone who calls the "sons of God" angels: they were sons of judges or nobles. Scholars think the rabbis set the book aside because of its non-rabbinic calendar, its use by sectarian groups and by Christians, and its picture of evil as caused by angels rather than by human choice. Some of its stories survived in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and the Talmud (Yoma 67b), and its Enoch became Metatron in 3 Enoch.

• Origen (about 230–250) used Enoch's words in On First Principles (1.3.3; 4.4.8) but wrote that the books under Enoch's name were not generally held as divine in the churches (Against Celsus 5.54) and spoke of it elsewhere as accepted only by those who wish.
  • Hilary of Poitiers (300s) mentioned the story, known from "some book," of angels who desired women and gathered on Mount Hermon, but said that since it is not in the book of the Law it should be passed over (on Psalm 133).
  • Jerome (392) wrote that Jude "is rejected by many" because it quotes "the apocryphal book of Enoch," but that it has earned its place in Scripture by age and use (Lives of Illustrious Men 4). He treated Enoch as apocryphal.
  • Augustine (about 420) wrote that Enoch surely wrote some inspired things, since Jude says so, but that the books under his name were rightly left out by the Jews and the church: they were too old to be trusted, their origin could not be proved, and they contained fables, such as the giants (City of God 15.23; also 18.38).
  • The Apostolic Constitutions (about 380) warn against "apocryphal books" of Moses, Enoch, Adam, Isaiah, David, Elijah and the three patriarchs as harmful and hostile to the truth (6.16).
  • The Stichometry of Nicephorus (800s) lists "Enoch" (4,800 lines) among the apocrypha of the Old Testament.
  • The Decretum Gelasianum (probably 500s) is often cited here, but its standard text, as far as I know, does not name 1 Enoch. It does reject a "book about the giant named Og" who fought a dragon after the Flood, which may come from the related giant traditions. This point should be treated as uncertain.

Writers who set the book aside gave or implied four main reasons. (1) Not received by Israel. Augustine and Jerome followed the Hebrew canon: the church received the Old Testament from the Jews, and they did not keep Enoch. (2) Doubtful origin. No one could show how a book written before the Flood survived. (3) Angels and women. From the 300s on, most teachers held that angels are spirits who cannot marry (Matthew 22:30), so the Watchers story seemed a fable (Chrysostom called it absurd). (4) Misuse. Some groups the church judged heretical, such as the Manichaeans, valued Enoch books, which made church leaders wary.

Modern scholars of every church, and of none, give historical reasons. Pseudonymity: the book was written in the name of an ancient figure, as many Jewish apocalypses were. Date: its parts reflect events and ideas of about 300 BC to the 1st century AD, such as Greek rule, the Maccabean revolt and perhaps the Parthians and Herod. Dependence: it builds on Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah and Ezekiel, so it was written after them. Content: its astronomy describes a flat earth with gates for the sun, its calendar is a solar year of 364 days that never matched the real year, and its angel lore goes far beyond the Bible's. Scholars note that these are reasons it is not by Enoch, not reasons it is worthless.

Tertullian (about 200) is the great defender. In On the Apparel of Women 1.3 he admits that some do not accept the book because it is not in the Jewish canon, and that some ask how it survived the Flood. He answers that Noah, Enoch's great-grandson, could have heard it at home and kept it, or, if it was destroyed, could have rewritten it by the Spirit, as Ezra was said to have restored the Scriptures. He adds that the Jews rejected it because it speaks of Christ, that Christians should reject nothing that concerns them, and that Jude, an apostle, quotes it. The Epistle of Barnabas cites Enoch as Scripture. The Ethiopian church kept it in its Bible and has never accepted the reasons above: for its teachers, Jude's word "prophesied," the book's own claims (82:1–2) and its long use in the church outweigh the doubts of other churches.

cited_in.b: The only direct quotation of 1 Enoch in the Bible, and the strongest link. Jude introduces it as prophecy by "Enoch, the seventh from Adam" (a phrase also in 60:8) and quotes 1:9 in a form close to the Greek of Codex Panopolitanus; the verse is also partly preserved in Aramaic in 4Q204. Jude changes "he" (God) to "the Lord," probably meaning Jesus. No one disputes that this is a quotation; churches disagree only about what it means for the book (see the card "Where Christians differ").

Angels who left their own dwelling, kept in chains in gloom for the great day of judgment. This matches the Watchers who left heaven (12:4; 15:3) and are bound in darkness until the day of judgment (10:4–6, 12–13). Almost all scholars see 1 Enoch behind this verse. Those who hold the Sethite view of Genesis 6 read Jude 6 as the first fall of angels instead, so the link is strong in wording but disputed in meaning.

"Wandering stars" kept for the blackest darkness echo the stars that broke God's command and were bound in a fiery prison (18:13–16; 21:1–6). Probable, since Jude has just quoted the book; widely accepted (Bauckham).

God did not spare the angels who sinned but threw them into Tartarus, in chains of gloom, kept for judgment. 2 Peter here reworks Jude 6, and through it the Watchers story (10:4–6, 12–13). The link is strong but indirect; 2 Peter does not quote Enoch.

Christ "preached to the spirits in prison" who disobeyed in Noah's day. Many scholars (Dalton, Elliott) read this against 1 Enoch 12–16, where Enoch goes to announce doom to the imprisoned Watchers: Christ goes as a greater Enoch to proclaim his victory to the fallen angels. Others follow Augustine (Christ preached through Noah to people of his day) or the old view that Christ preached to the dead in Hades. A real possibility, but disputed.

The reverse direction: 1 Enoch builds on Genesis. Genesis says only that Enoch walked with God for 300 years, lived 365 years, and "was gone, for God took him." The Hebrew "walked with God" (literally "with the God" or "with the angels," et-ha'elohim) and "took" invited the idea that Enoch lived among heavenly beings and was taken to heaven, which 1 Enoch develops (12:1–2; 70–71). Ethiopian Orthodox teachers see the opposite relation: Genesis briefly records the man whose own books 1 Enoch preserves.

1 Enoch 6–11 retells these verses at length: the "sons of God" become 200 Watchers, the Nephilim become giants, and the violence of Genesis 6:11 becomes the giants' doing. Most scholars think Enoch expands Genesis; Milik and a few others argued that Genesis 6:1–4 abbreviates an older story like Enoch's. Either way, 1 Enoch is the oldest surviving interpretation of the passage.

The reverse direction again. The goat "for Azazel" on the Day of Atonement carries the people's sins into the wilderness. 1 Enoch makes Azazel the angel who taught sin, bound in the desert of Dudael and blamed for all sin (10:4–8). Scholars see Enoch borrowing the name and the scapegoat imagery from Leviticus.

The opening of 1 Enoch is built from older Scripture: "the blessing" (Deuteronomy 33:1), God coming from Sinai with myriads of holy ones (Deuteronomy 33:2), and the coming of God with all his holy ones (Zechariah 14:5). Balaam's oracles shape 1:2–3 (Numbers 24:3–4, 15–17). So Jude's quotation is itself an Enochic reading of the Torah.

Daniel's Ancient of Days with clothing white as snow, a fiery throne with wheels, streams of fire, and thousands upon thousands serving him closely match Enoch's throne vision (14:18–22), which most date earlier than Daniel. Many scholars (Nickelsburg, Kvanvig) think Daniel drew on the Book of the Watchers or on a shared tradition; others think both drew on Ezekiel 1. The Parables (46–48) in turn clearly build on Daniel 7's "one like a son of man."

"The Son of Man takes his seat on the throne of his glory." The Parables use the same phrase again and again for the seat where the Chosen One, the Son of Man, judges (45:3; 55:4; 62:2–5; 69:27–29). In the Hebrew Bible a throne of glory is God's (Jeremiah 17:12). Many scholars think Matthew's wording reflects the Parables or the tradition behind them. The link depends on the Parables' date: if they are before Jesus, the link is likely; if later, the dependence could run the other way or be a shared Jewish idea.

The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, sits on his throne of glory, and judges the nations, separating righteous from wicked. This is the closest New Testament parallel to the Parables' scenes of the Chosen One on the throne judging the kings and the mighty (61:8; 62:2–16). Strong in theme; direct dependence is debated for the same reason as Matthew 19:28.

The Father has given all judgment to the Son, "because he is the Son of Man." In 69:27 the whole judgment is given to the Son of Man. A possible echo of the Parables; many see only shared Jewish tradition built on Daniel 7.

"It would have been better for that man if he had not been born." 38:2 says much the same of sinners who deny the Lord of Spirits. A possible verbal echo; the saying may simply be a common Jewish expression.

In the story of the rich man and Lazarus, the dead are in separate places, with a great gap between them, and the righteous have comfort and water while the wicked are in torment. 1 Enoch 22 has the oldest Jewish picture of the dead kept in separate hollow places until judgment, with a bright spring of water for the righteous. Shared Jewish belief rather than quotation; few claim direct use.

At the transfiguration the voice says, "This is my Son, the Chosen One" (in the oldest manuscripts). "The Chosen One" is the Parables' favorite title for the heavenly judge (40:5; 45:3; 49:2). Isaiah 42:1 is the more common explanation; a link with the Parables is possible but disputed.

Jesus' woes on the rich, the full and those who laugh now resemble the Epistle's long series of woes on the rich who trust in wealth (94:8; 96:4–8; 97:8–10). James 5:1–6 is closer still. Most scholars see a shared Jewish tradition of woes, with the Epistle as an important earlier example.

Weep, you rich; your wealth will testify against you; you fattened yourselves for a day of slaughter. Very close in theme and some images to 94:7–11; 97:8–10; 98:2; 100:7. A shared tradition, possibly a direct influence; disputed.

In the resurrection people do not marry but are like the angels in heaven. 15:6–7 says the spirits of heaven were never given wives, because they do not die. Augustine and others later used Jesus' saying against the Watchers story; scholars note that 1 Enoch itself agrees that angels were not meant to marry, which is why the Watchers' act was a crime.

A woman should have authority on her head "because of the angels." Tertullian and some modern scholars read this against the Watchers who desired women; most scholars today think Paul means the angels present in worship. Disputed and uncertain.

Enoch was taken so that he did not see death, and before that he was commended as one who pleased God. Hebrews follows the Greek of Genesis 5:24 ("he pleased God... he was not found"), not 1 Enoch. It shares the belief, also in Sirach 44:16 and Wisdom of Solomon 4:10, that Enoch did not die. Weak as a link to 1 Enoch.

An angel binds Satan with a great chain and throws him into the abyss, sealed until his release and final punishment. The binding of Azazel and Shemihazah, thrown into darkness until the great day (10:4–6, 11–13), and the stars bound in an abyss of fire (18:11–16; 21:7–10; 88:1–3) are the closest Jewish parallels. A probable allusion to the tradition, though the details differ.

The souls of the martyrs cry out "How long?" and are told to wait until the number of their fellow servants is complete. 47:1–4 has the blood of the righteous going up to God, and the holy ones rejoicing when the number of the righteous is reached. Many scholars (Charles, Bauckham) see this as an Enochic theme Revelation uses.

Blood flows as high as horses' bridles. 100:3 says a horse will walk up to its chest in the blood of sinners. A striking and specific parallel that many commentators note; perhaps a shared image of war.

A throne, books opened, the dead judged, and the wicked thrown into fire. 90:20–27 has a throne set up, the sealed books opened, and the fallen stars and the blind sheep thrown into a fiery abyss. Daniel 7:9–10 lies behind both; the shared picture is clear, direct use is uncertain.
A new heaven and a new earth; the first heaven passed away. The Apocalypse of Weeks says the first heaven will pass away and a new heaven appear (91:16). Both build on Isaiah 65:17 and Isaiah 66:22.

The vision of God's throne room in heaven, with fire, crystal and countless worshipers. 1 Enoch 14 and 71 are the oldest Jewish throne visions after Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6, and Revelation 4 belongs to the same tradition. Shared tradition, not quotation.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what many Jews believed in the three centuries before Jesus, 1 Enoch is among the most valuable books we have: its oldest parts are dated by actual manuscripts from about 200 BC, and its ideas appear in Jude, 1 and 2 Peter, the Gospels' Son of Man sayings and Revelation. As a text, it survived unevenly: complete only in a Ge'ez translation of a Greek translation of an Aramaic original, with the oldest complete copies from the 1400s, though the Greek and Aramaic let scholars check about a third of it. As history, its claim to come from Enoch before the Flood is not supported by the evidence, which points to Jewish writers of about 300 BC to the 1st century AD; Ethiopian Orthodox teachers answer that God preserved Enoch's words, and that Jude confirms them. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees on the core (one holy God, judgment, resurrection hope, God's care for the righteous) and goes well beyond them on angels, the calendar and the cosmos, and in a few places it conflicts with how most churches read the Bible.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish belief before Jesus: very high
sections.b: Here the book's value is not in doubt for anyone. The Qumran fragments prove that the Watchers and the Astronomical Book were being copied by about 200 BC, the Dream Visions by about 150 BC, and the Epistle in the 1st century BC. That makes it older than most other Jewish writings outside the Hebrew Bible. It shows ideas that the New Testament takes for granted but the Old Testament hardly explains: fallen angels held for judgment, demons as the spirits of the giants (15:8–12), named archangels (Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel), separate places for the dead before judgment (22), the resurrection and the final judgment of all, and a heavenly Son of Man who judges (46–48; 62; 69). When Jesus spoke of the Son of Man on his throne of glory, or Jude of angels in chains, many hearers would have known these ideas from Enoch's books. For understanding the world of the New Testament, it is essential.

Mixed. The good news: there are three independent lines of evidence (Aramaic, Greek, Ge'ez), and where they overlap they usually agree in substance, which shows the Ge'ez is a real translation of the ancient book, not a medieval invention. The bad news: the Aramaic is in small pieces and covers perhaps a fifth of the book; the Greek covers about a third; and for the Parables (37–71) and chapter 108 we have only Ge'ez. The Ge'ez is a translation of a translation, its oldest copies are from the 1400s, and the later Ethiopic II family smoothed the text. The Astronomical Book in Ge'ez is a shortened form of a much longer Aramaic work, and the Apocalypse of Weeks was put out of order (93:1–10 belongs before 91:11–17). Scholars can usually tell what the book said, but in many verses the exact wording is uncertain, and the variant notes say so. Compared with the books of the Bible, whose copies are far older and more numerous, the text of 1 Enoch is much less secure.

sections.h: 3. The claim to be by Enoch
sections.b: The book says Enoch wrote it before the Flood. The historical evidence points the other way. The parts reflect events of their own times (the Maccabean revolt in 89–90, probably the Parthians in 56); they build on books written long after any date for Enoch (Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel); they differ from one another in style and ideas; and they first appear in manuscripts from about 200 BC. Writing in the name of an ancient hero was common in Jewish writings of the time, and most scholars do not see it as fraud but as a claim to speak in the tradition of a righteous man of old. The Ethiopian Orthodox answer, in its strongest form: God can preserve a prophecy through Noah and his descendants, as the book itself says (82:1–2) and as Tertullian argued; Jude, an inspired writer, calls the words Enoch's prophecy; and a book's late appearance in manuscripts does not prove its late origin. Those who hold this view would add that scholars' dates depend on reading prophecy as history written after the event. A fair summary: the evidence of language, sources and events strongly favors later Jewish authors, and the traditional view rests on faith in the church's reception and Jude's words rather than on historical evidence.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: one holy, eternal God who made all things and judges all (1:3–9; 9:4–11); judgment on the wicked and vindication of the righteous; concern for the poor against the oppressive rich (94–100, like Amos, Luke 6 and James 5); the Flood as judgment (Genesis 6–9); resurrection and life after death (51:1; 91:10; 92:3; 104:2, like Daniel 12:2–3).
  • Goes beyond: the names and numbers of the fallen angels and their teachings (6–8); the giants' spirits as demons (15:8–12); detailed geography of heaven and the underworld (17–36); a heavenly Son of Man who existed before creation (48:2–6; 62:7). Christians who do not count the book as Scripture read these as Jewish beliefs, some of which the New Testament uses (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4) and many of which it never confirms.
  • Differs or conflicts: (a) The 364-day calendar (72–82), which the book says is the only true one (82:4–7), against the calendar used in the Temple and assumed in the Bible's feasts. (b) Evil's origin: the Watchers' sin is the main cause of human wickedness (9:6–9; 10:8), while Genesis 3 and Paul (Romans 5:12) trace sin to Adam. The book itself also says people made sin themselves (98:4), so the tension is real but not total. (c) Enoch as the Son of Man (71:14, in the usual reading) against the New Testament's identification of the Son of Man with Jesus. (d) Its cosmology of gates in the sky and a flat earth with its ends, though the Bible also uses the picture language of its time. (e) Its teaching that the Watchers cannot be forgiven (12:4–6; 14:4–7), which some contrast with the Bible's wide offer of mercy, though the Bible too speaks of angels kept for judgment.
  • Each church's view: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox read the book in harmony with the rest of Scripture through their tradition: the calendar passages are read as about God's order in creation rather than as binding against the church's calendar, and 71:14 and the Son of Man passages are read as prophecy of Christ, in whom Enoch's hope is fulfilled. Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, other Oriental Orthodox and Protestant teachers read it as a human book that often witnesses to truth and sometimes errs, to be tested by the canon. Many scholars of every background see its differences from the Bible as part of the variety of Jewish thought in the Second Temple period.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you belong to the Ethiopian or Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, it is part of your Bible, and your church's teachers and its commentary tradition are your guide. If you belong to another church, it is not Scripture for you, but it is an ancient and serious Jewish book that the New Testament writers knew. Either way, read it with respect, and do not treat it as a secret key that unlocks hidden meanings of the Bible.

how_to_read.h: Start with the Bible passages it builds on
how_to_read.b: Read Genesis 5:18–6:8, then 1 Enoch 1–16, then Jude and 2 Peter 2. Next read Daniel 7, then the Parables (37–71), then Matthew 25:31–46. You will see how one story grows from a few verses in Genesis, how the Son of Man of Daniel becomes the judge on the throne of glory, and how the New Testament uses some of that language.

how_to_read.h: Read each part in its own time
how_to_read.b: Ask, for each of the five books, who first read it and what they were afraid of: Greek rule and its new ideas (the Watchers), a persecuting king (the Dream Visions), the rich and powerful (the Epistle), Roman and Herodian rulers (the Parables). The book's strange images are usually answers to those fears: God is in control, the wicked will be judged, and the faithful will shine.

how_to_read.h: Test it, and let it test you
how_to_read.b: Readers who do not count it as Scripture can do what the early church did with such books: weigh it against the canon, keep what agrees, and set aside what does not. Use the "Compared with the Bible" notes for that. But also let it challenge you. Its anger at the abuse of wealth and power, its belief that God sees and records every injustice, and its hope that the righteous will be raised are close to the heart of the Bible.

Many books, videos and websites make big claims about 1 Enoch: that it was "banned" from the Bible, that it reveals hidden history about giants, or that the church suppressed it. The real history is quieter. It was never in the Jewish Bible or in any Greek or Latin Bible; it was widely read for a few centuries, slowly set aside outside Ethiopia for the reasons on this page, and faithfully kept in Ethiopia. When a claim sounds dramatic, check the dates and the sources given here.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "1 Enoch, an ancient Jewish book that Jude quotes, and Scripture for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches." When you teach Jude, 1 Peter 3, 2 Peter 2 or the Son of Man sayings, 1 Enoch is the best background there is. When churches disagree about it, as on the giants of Genesis 6, set out each view fairly, as the cards on these pages do.
